1Tool application

A Power BI dashboard shows new starters and overtime workers are most likely to leave

16.1%overall attrition237 of 1,470 employees
30.5%attrition with overtimevs 10.4% without
29.8%attrition in first 2 yearsvs 8.1% after 11+ years
39.8%Sales Representativesthe highest-risk role

Business scenario

A mid-sized company's HR team knows staff turnover is rising but cannot say where or why. Exit data sits in spreadsheets and managers rely on anecdotes. I used Microsoft Power BI with the IBM HR Analytics Attrition dataset, a fictional dataset of 1,470 employees created by IBM data scientists, to show how a dashboard turns this data into evidence for decisions.

How the tool was applied

The CSV file was loaded into Power BI and cleaned in Power Query: data types were fixed and ages and tenure grouped into bands. A DAX measure calculates the attrition rate, and slicers let managers filter by department, job role, age band, overtime and gender.

Attrition Rate =
DIVIDE(
    CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(HR), HR[Attrition] = "Yes"),
    COUNTROWS(HR)
)

Insights and business value

Overtime workers leave 2.9 times as often as colleagues who do not work overtime. Attrition is highest in the first two years and among Sales Representatives. HR can move from guesswork to targeted action: reviewing Sales workloads and strengthening onboarding, rather than funding company-wide schemes. Because replacing an employee costs a large share of their salary, even small reductions in turnover produce real savings.

Limitations

  • The dashboard is descriptive: overtime and leaving occur together, which does not prove one causes the other.
  • Employee data is personal data under UK GDPR, so access must be restricted and results aggregated.
  • The same data could label individuals as "flight risks" without their knowledge. I would avoid this without transparency, a concern developed in Parts 2 and 4.
2Case analysis

Amazon's recruiting AI learned to prefer men from ten years of its own hiring

From 2014, Amazon built a machine-learning tool that rated applicants from one to five stars. Trained on a decade of CVs, mostly from men, it taught itself that male candidates were preferable and was abandoned in early 2017 (Reuters, 2018).

What happened

By 2015 Amazon realised the system was not rating technical candidates in a gender-neutral way. It penalised CVs containing the word "women's", as in "women's chess club captain", and downgraded graduates of all-women's colleges. Engineers edited the model to treat these terms neutrally but could not guarantee it would not find other ways to discriminate. Amazon stated the tool was never used by recruiters to evaluate candidates.

Why it matters

The model did exactly what it was trained to do: it reproduced past patterns. Removing one word did not remove correlated signals such as college names or wording. This is proxy discrimination, and it shows that a technically "working" model can still be an ethical and commercial failure.

Implications for business performance

  • Several years of specialist effort produced no usable tool.
  • Filtering out qualified women shrinks the talent pool in a sector short of engineers.
  • Global coverage of "sexist AI" damaged the employer brand.
  • In the UK, a similar tool could lead to indirect discrimination claims under the Equality Act 2010.

Ethical implications

  • The failure came from uncritical trust in historical data, not malicious intent.
  • The system was opaque, so rejected candidates could not know or challenge their scores.
  • Accountability was unclear: who answers for an algorithm's decision?
  • Credit is due: internal testing found the problem and Amazon stopped the project.
Lesson for businesses: audit outcomes by group before deployment, keep trained people accountable for every hiring decision, and never accept "it was the algorithm" as a defence.
3Digital strategy insight

Generative AI in recruitment pays off in support tasks and becomes risky when it judges people

72%of HR professionals used AI weekly in 2025up from 58% in 2024 · HireVue
91%of US HR leaders use AI in recruitmentPaylocity, 1,000+ leaders
71%think most applications are AI-writtenPaylocity
98%don't fully trust AI with workforce decisionsAvature, 2025

Business potential

Generative AI handles high-volume, low-judgement work well: drafting inclusive job adverts, personalising candidate outreach, summarising interview notes and answering applicants' questions at any hour. Recruiters gain time for relationships and final assessment, and businesses gain a shorter time-to-hire and lower cost-per-hire.

Risks

Ranking candidates can repeat the Amazon pattern from Part 2. When most applications are AI-written, CVs become weaker signals of ability. Regulation is also tightening: the EU AI Act classes recruitment AI as high-risk. The Digital Omnibus on AI (July 2026) moved these obligations to 2 December 2027 but did not remove them.

Recommendation: a staged strategy

  1. Assist

    Adopt generative AI first for drafting, scheduling and candidate communication.

  2. Screen with safeguards

    Use AI screening only with bias audits, transparency to candidates and a named human decision-maker.

  3. Prepare for 2027

    Use the time before the EU AI Act deadline to build governance, not to postpone it.

4Reflective summary

I began seeing AI as a way to remove human judgement. I finish seeing it as a way to strengthen it.

Before the module

AI as an objective efficiency tool

→
After the module

AI as support for accountable human decisions

How my understanding evolved

At the start of the module I saw AI mainly as an efficiency tool that could screen hundreds of CVs in seconds and remove human inconsistency. I assumed that data-driven meant objective. Building the turnover dashboard changed this view: every chart depends on choices about which data is collected, how categories are defined and which questions a manager asks.

The Amazon case made this concrete. Nothing in the algorithm was "broken"; it faithfully reproduced past patterns. I now understand digital management as the governance of data, people and processes around a tool, not only the choice of tool.

Ethical and societal insights

Bias in AI hiring is harder to see, and so harder to challenge, than bias in one interviewer. A biased manager affects a few candidates; a biased algorithm can affect thousands, quietly and at scale. Rejected candidates rarely know why, which weakens their ability to contest decisions.

"Human in the loop" can also become a box-ticking exercise. If recruiters approve whatever the system ranks highest, oversight exists on paper only. Meaningful oversight needs people with the time, training and authority to question the output.

How I will apply this in my career

  • Question the data firstAsk what historical data a model learned from, and whose experience it leaves out.
  • Keep humans accountableAI can shortlist, summarise or flag patterns; final decisions rest with a trained person who can explain them.
  • Monitor outcomes, not just accuracyTrack results such as shortlist rates by gender, age and ethnicity, using dashboards like the one in Part 1, to catch unfair patterns early.

Fair hiring with AI is possible, but only when organisations treat fairness and oversight as part of the design rather than an afterthought.
